1.note: The word **And** introduces a new section of Moses’ instructions. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a connecting word that specifically signals the start of a new topic. Alternate translation: [Then Moses and the elders of Israel commanded] or [Now Moses and the elders of Israel commanded]

Here the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly since **commanded** already implies speaking. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

The pronoun **I** refers to Moses. Even though Moses and the elders are both commanding the people, Moses is the only one speaking. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Moses, command]
The word **you** is plural here because Moses is addressing the Israelites, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

2.q: בַּ⁠יּוֹם֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תַּעַבְר֣וּ אֶת־הַ⁠יַּרְדֵּן֒ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֕רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖י⁠ךָ נֹתֵ֣ן לָ֑⁠ךְ וַ⁠הֲקֵמֹתָ֤
2.note: Moses expected the Israelites to erect these stones at the same time as when they crossed the Jordan. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [as soon as you cross the Jordan into the land that Yahweh your God is giving to you, you shall erect]
The word **you** is plural here because Moses is addressing the Israelites, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
See how you translated the phrase “Yahweh your God” in 1:10.

A **plaster** is a kind of material made from lime, sand, and water that hardens after it dries. If your readers would not be familiar with what plaster is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and cover them with a smooth coating] or [and coat them with a material that hardens]

Moses is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and thoroughly cover them with a lime coating] or [and completely coat them with plaster]

3.note: Here, **so that** marks entering the land as the goal or purpose of writing the law on the stones. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to enter the land]
See how you translated the phrase “a land flowing with milk and honey” in 6:3.
Moses is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the God of your ancestors]

4.note: This is a mountain near Mount Gerizim near the town of Shechem. See how you translated it in 11:29.
The word **you** is plural here, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
See how you translated this in 27:2.

5.note: The implication is that an iron tool would shape or carve the stones, and this would make them unacceptable as an altar to Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you shall not shape these stones with an iron tool]

7.note: Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. See the Introduction to Deuteronomy for a discussion about this phrase. See how you translated it in 1:45. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh your God]

10.note: Here, **voice** represents what Yahweh says or commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And hear what Yahweh your God commands] or [And hear what Yahweh your God says]
See how you translated the similar expression “his statutes and his commandments” in 4:40.

12.note: A small mountain north of Mount Ebal. See how you translated this in 11:29.
The word **you** is plural here, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

12.q: שִׁמְעוֹן֙ וְ⁠לֵוִ֣י וִֽ⁠יהוּדָ֔ה וְ⁠יִשָּׂשכָ֖ר וְ⁠יוֹסֵ֥ף וּ⁠בִנְיָמִֽן
12.note: Moses is using **Simeon and Levi and Judah and Issachar and Joseph and Benjamin** to represent the tribes that were descended from these men. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.
The name **Joseph** combines the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, who were descendants of Joseph.

13.note: The implication is that the tribes who are to stand on Mount Ebal will listen to the curse statements that are listed in verses 15–26. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And these tribes shall stand to hear the curses]

13.q: רְאוּבֵן֙ גָּ֣ד וְ⁠אָשֵׁ֔ר וּ⁠זְבוּלֻ֖ן דָּ֥ן וְ⁠נַפְתָּלִֽי
13.note: Moses is using **Reuben, Gad and Asher and Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali** to represent the tribes descended from these men. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

14.note: Moses is instructing the Levites to **respond** with the following statement as part of this ceremony, rather than as an answer to what someone said to them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Levites shall say]

The phrase **and say** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. Alternate translation: [And the Levites shall respond]

Here the masculine term **men** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [all the people of Israel]

15.note: The expression **Cursed is the man who** contains a passive verbal form that appears in every verse through verse 26. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form as modeled in the UST or in another way that is natural in your language.

15.q: אָר֣וּר הָ⁠אִ֡ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר & וְ⁠עָנ֧וּ כָל־הָ⁠עָ֛ם וְ⁠אָמְר֖וּ אָמֵֽן
15.note: Throughout this passage, Moses and the Levites use a repeated pattern: they declare a curse and the people respond with **Amen**. If your language has a way of repeating patterns of speech and response, you could use it here.

The speakers are not referring to a specific **man** but rather any person in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is anyone who]

A **cast figure** is a kind of idol made by pouring hot metal into a mold. If your readers would not be familiar with what a cast figure is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [or metal idol] or [or statue made from melted metal]

The Levites are using one part of a person, his **hands**, to mean all of him in the act of making idols. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what a craftsman has made]

The word **Amen** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Let it be so] or [We agree]

16.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who dishonors]

17.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who displaces]

The implication is that a person moves **boundary** markers in order to steal land from a neighbor. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is the one who steals land from his neighbor by moving the boundary markers]

18.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who misleads]

19.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who twists]

Here the speakers are describing **judgment** as if it were something that could be physically twisted. By this expression, they are referring to someone who is perverting justice. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is the one who perverts justice of] or [is the one who makes an unfair judgment of]

The Levites are referring to all vulnerable people by naming three representative groups, **a foreigner**, **fatherless**, and **widow**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [anyone who is helpless]

Here, **a foreigner, fatherless, or widow** represent vulnerable people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any vulnerable person]

20.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who lies]
See how you translated “lies with” in 22:23. Alternate translation: [is the one who sleeps with] or [is the one who is intimate with]

The phrase **the wife of his father** refers to a woman who is married to a man’s father but who is not the man’s mother. Your language may have its own term or expression for this relationship. Alternate translation: [his stepmother]

The Levites are using **uncovered the hem of his father** as a common expression of their culture to mean “disrespect his father by violating his father’s marriage rights.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has disrespected his father]

21.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who lies]
See how you translated “lies with” in 22:23. Alternate translation: [is the one who sleeps with] or [is the one who is intimate with]

22.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who lies]
See how you translated “lies with” in 22:23. Alternate translation: [is the one who sleeps with] or [is the one who is intimate with]

The implication is that this means any kind of **sister**, whether from the same mother and father, or sharing only one parent. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his sister, whether they share both parents or only one]
See how you translated “lies with” in 22:23. Alternate translation: [is the one who sleeps with] or [is the one who is intimate with]

23.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who lies]
See how you translated “lies with” in 22:23. Alternate translation: [is the one who sleeps with] or [is the one who is intimate with]
Your language may have its own term or expression for the relationship described by **mother-in-law** which here means the mother of a man’s wife. Alternate translation: [his wife’s mother]

24.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who strikes]

Here the term **strikes** means attacking with the intent to kill. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is the one who murders his neighbor in secret]

25.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one who takes]

The Levites are using **to strike a life of innocent blood** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to murder an innocent person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to murder an innocent person]

Here, **innocent blood** represents the life of an innocent person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [an innocent person] or [someone who has done nothing wrong]

26.note: See how you translated the similar passive expression, “Cursed is the man who” in 27:15. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh curse the one]

Here, **words** represents the commands of the law. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the commands of this law] or [the requirements of this law]
